name: lifefrom-units
notice: Not a medical device. Converts units only; it does not interpret results.
ucum_notice: UCUM code strings are expressions in the Unified Code for Units of Measure, Copyright 1999-2024 Regenstrief Institute, Inc., used under the UCUM License (https://ucum.org/license). This mapping from lab spellings to UCUM codes is not part of UCUM and is not a units standard.

rules.note: Greek small mu (U+03BC) to micro sign (U+00B5)
Greek capital mu used as micro
thin, narrow and non-breaking spaces to space

normalization.procedure: key = rules applied in order to the trimmed input, then all whitespace removed. Look up key in lookup.exact; if absent, apply the same to the lower-cased input and look up in lookup.ambiguous, then in lookup.casefold. A spelling found in lookup.ambiguous resolves only with a locale whose primary language subtag (lower-cased, e.g. 'es' from 'es-AR') is in that entry's readings; otherwise it is refused (ambiguous_unit).

ambiguous.reason: 'mil' means thousand in Spanish ('7,5 mil/mm3' white cells = 7.5 × 10^3/mm³) but million on English and Romanian reports ('4.5 Mil/µL' red cells = 4.5 × 10^6/µL), a factor of 1000 apart.
'mil' means thousand in Spanish ('7,5 mil/mm3' white cells = 7.5 × 10^3/mm³) but million on English and Romanian reports ('4.5 Mil/µL' red cells = 4.5 × 10^6/µL), a factor of 1000 apart.

es.note: Spanish: 'mil' is the numeral one thousand (miles = thousands), so 'mil/mm3' = 10^3/mm³. Spanish has no conventional abbreviation for millón; millions are written out ('millones') or shortened to 'mill.'. Spanish-language documents translated from US usage can still use 'mil' for million (NIH Clinical Center), so pass locale='es' only for reports that follow Spanish usage.

en.note: English (US reports): 'Mil' abbreviates million, for example red cell counts in 'mil/uL'.

ro.note: Romanian: 'mil.' is read as an abbreviation of milion (plural milioane); thousands are 'mii' (plural of mie). No dictionary entry for the abbreviation 'mil.' itself was found; the reading rests on the two numerals.

forbidden.reason: Lp(a) mass (mg/dL) and particle concentration (nmol/L) measure different things. Apolipoprotein(a) size varies between people, and assays vary, so there is no fixed factor.
Insulin µIU/mL to pmol/L factors differ by assay and manufacturer (6.0 is common, others are in use). Convert only with the factor stated by the assay that produced the result.

AMH is a glycoprotein with no formula-based molar mass. NHANES 2021-2023 (TST_L) converts ng/mL to pmol/L by multiplying by 7.14, but does not state that the factor is assay-independent. lifefrom-units does not apply it by default; pass factor= with the factor your assay states.
% and mmol/mol cannot be converted by a unit factor. For HbA1c, NGSP % and IFCC mmol/mol are related by the IFCC-NGSP master equation: pass analyte='hba1c'.
HbA1c NGSP % is a calibrated scale tied to the DCCT, not a true fraction of total haemoglobin. Use % or mmol/mol for HbA1c, not a fraction of 1.
IU are used for vitamin D intake and doses. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is reported in ng/mL or nmol/L; there is no IU concentration for it.

arbitrary_reason: Arbitrary (assay-defined) units are not commensurable with any other unit; results in different arbitrary units, or from different assays, cannot be converted.
